name: Abimelech son of Gideon
charge: Murder of seventy brothers on one stone; usurping a crown
summary: Gideon's son by a Shechemite concubine hired vain and light persons with silver from the house of Baal-berith, killed his seventy brothers on one stone, and had himself made king at Shechem. Only Jotham escaped, and his parable from Mount Gerizim pronounced the sentence.
offense: Abimelech appealed to his mother's brethren in Shechem and asked whether they preferred seventy sons of Jerubbaal to rule them or one man who was their own bone and flesh (Judges 9:1-2). They promoted him because he was their brother. Kinship took the place of judgment, and money from the house of Baal-berith financed the choice: seventy pieces of silver paid the vain and light men who followed him (Judges 9:3-4). He went to his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren upon one stone; Jotham escaped by hiding. Shechem then made the killer king (Judges 9:5-6). Their part was not confined to approving him afterward. They supplied the means by which he established his rule. The blood would be laid upon the man who killed and upon the men who strengthened his hands (Judges 9:24). Jotham spoke from Mount Gerizim. In his parable, the olive, fig, and vine would not forsake their fruitfulness to reign over the trees, but the bramble offered its shadow and threatened fire (Judges 9:7-15). He applied it to the ingratitude shown his father's house: Gideon had risked his life to deliver them, and they had answered by destroying his sons. If their choice was not true and sincere, Abimelech and Shechem would consume one another (Judges 9:16-20).
judgment: Three years passed before the alliance broke. God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem so that the blood of Gideon's sons would be requited upon both parties (Judges 9:22-24). The interval had not erased the murder. Numbers 32:23 warns that sin will find the offender out; a season of apparent success is not acquittal. Shechem dealt treacherously, trusted Gaal, and cursed Abimelech; Abimelech returned with ambush and slaughter. He destroyed the city and burned the stronghold where about a thousand men and women had taken refuge (Judges 9:26-49). The man they had called their brother brought the fire Jotham had pronounced. The god whose treasury financed his rise could not shelter those who fled into its house. At Thebez, Abimelech approached another tower to burn it, but a woman cast a piece of millstone upon his head and crushed his skull. He ordered his armour-bearer to kill him so that men would not say a woman slew him (Judges 9:50-54). Even at death he sought control of his reputation. The history still records the woman and the stone. God rendered Abimelech's wickedness upon him and Shechem's evil upon its own head; Jotham's curse came upon them (Judges 9:56-57). The killer and his backers did not cancel one another's guilt by becoming enemies. Their conflict became the means by which both were repaid.

verses.text: And Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem unto his mother’s brethren, and communed with them, and with all the family of the house of his mother’s father, saying,

Speak, I pray you, in the ears of all the men of Shechem, Whether is better for you, either that all the sons of Jerubbaal, which are threescore and ten persons, reign over you, or that one reign over you? remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.
And his mother’s brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem all these words: and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech; for they said, He is our brother.
And they gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal–berith, wherewith Abimelech hired vain and light persons, which followed him.

And he went unto his father’s house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
And all the men of Shechem gathered together, and all the house of Millo, and went, and made Abimelech king, by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem.

Now therefore, if ye have done truly and sincerely, in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, and have done unto him according to the deserving of his hands;
(For my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian:

And ye are risen up against my father’s house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother;)
If ye then have dealt truly and sincerely with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you:
But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem, and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem, and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.
When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel,
Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech:

That the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them; and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren.
And Abimelech fought against the city all that day; and he took the city, and slew the people that was therein, and beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.
And Abimelech came unto the tower, and fought against it, and went hard unto the door of the tower to burn it with fire.
And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech’s head, and all to brake his skull.

Then he called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer, and said unto him, Draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. And his young man thrust him through, and he died.
And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they departed every man unto his place.
Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren:
And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.

Who smote Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? did not a woman cast a piece of a millstone upon him from the wall, that he died in Thebez? why went ye nigh the wall? then say thou, Thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.

entries.commentary: Abimelech was the son of Jerubbaal by his concubine in Shechem. He went to Shechem unto his mother's brethren, his uncles on his mother's side, and had them ask the men of Shechem whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to reign over them, or for one man to reign. Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh: he reminded them that he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

His mother's brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem, whispering for their nephew, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, He is our brother. They chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol's house to back his rise. Politics has always worked this way: people will put a man in office not because he is best for the job, but because he is family or because they know him. Baal was the chief god of the Canaanites, worshipped as the god of the elements who brought rain and made the ground fruitful, and sometimes as the god of war. Baal-berith, also called El-berith, was the Canaanite god of Shechem in the twelfth century BC, a sub god under Baal. With that money Abimelech hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, which followed him.

He went unto his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone. He killed his own family to clear his way to a throne. Notwithstanding, Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.

All the men of Shechem and all the house of Millo gathered together and made Abimelech king by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem. They endorsed the man who had just used their money and his hired men to murder his seventy brothers.

When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood in the top of mount Gerizim, lifted up his voice, and cried, Hearken unto me, ye men of Shechem, that God may hearken unto you. This young brother was fearless; he stood up alone and rebuked the men who had made his brothers' killer king. In his parable the trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them. The olive tree would not leave its fatness, wherewith by it they honour God and man; the fig tree would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; the vine would not leave its wine, which cheereth God and man. The profitable trees refused to be promoted over the trees. Only the bramble accepted: if in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon. The worthless bush took the crown, and its answer carried the threat of fire.

Jotham applied the parable: if ye have done truly and sincerely in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. He reminded them of what they owed his father: my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian; and ye are risen up against my father's house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother. They did it only because he was kin to them. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech. That is what the parable of the bramble was about: he prophesied that they would destroy one another, and it came to pass.
Jotham ran away and fled to Beer and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother. His brother already had a reputation for killing; he knew he could be next.

When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech. Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody's spirit suddenly changes toward you, we tend to think it is just that person; the scripture shows the Most High is the one who stirs these things. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world's false ideas and idols. The Most High is in the midst of these things, mustering the host, the armies above and below, and he even puts it on the spirit of one wicked man to go against another. The reason is given: that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them, and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren. The hired men and the backers carried the blood guilt too. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.
The men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains, and they robbed all that came along that way by them; and it was told Abimelech. The treachery the Most High sent had begun.

Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren and went over to Shechem, and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him. They went out into the fields, gathered their vineyards, trode the grapes, made merry, went into the house of their god, did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech. Gaal talked big: who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer? serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him? He asked why they should be serving this Israelite at all. Would to God this people were under my hand! then would I remove Abimelech. He was talking cash money with wine in him: increase thine army, and come out.

When Zebul the ruler of the city, Abimelech's officer, heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. He sent messengers unto Abimelech privily, saying, Behold, Gaal and his brethren fortify the city against thee. Zebul counselled Abimelech to rise up by night with his people and lie in wait in the field, and in the morning, as soon as the sun was up, to set upon the city. This is the same hand we read of in verse 23; the Lord is in the midst of this whole treachery, turning it back on all of them.

Abimelech and all the people with him rose up by night and laid wait against Shechem in four companies. When Gaal saw the people coming down from the top of the mountains, Zebul told him, Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men, playing him until it was too late. Then Zebul threw his own words back at him: where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? is not this the people that thou hast despised? go out, I pray now, and fight with them. All of that big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Gaal went out before the men of Shechem and fought with Abimelech, and Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many were overthrown and wounded, even unto the entering of the gate. Abimelech dwelt at Arumah, and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.

On the morrow the people went out into the field, and it was told Abimelech. He divided his men into three companies, laid wait in the field, rose up against the people, and smote them. Abimelech fought against the city all that day; he took the city, slew the people that was therein, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.

When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard that, they entered into an hold of the house of the god Berith. Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, cut down a bough from the trees with an axe, laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done. They cut every man his bough, put them to the hold, and set the hold on fire upon them, so that all the men of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women. Remember, these are the people whose money and endorsement made him king: I am your brother, make me king. Now he turned on Shechem itself and burned them; the fire out of the bramble that Jotham prophesied was devouring the men of Shechem.

Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled to the top of it. Abimelech came unto the tower and went hard unto the door to burn it with fire, and a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull. A millstone is a heavy stone; it crushed his skull. He called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer: draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death earlier in this book. His young man thrust him through, and he died. He reigned only three years. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. If you are doing wickedness behind closed doors and think the Most High does not see it, he sees it, and he brings swift judgment.

Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren; and all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads. Both sides were judged; for three years they reigned and everything looked good, then the Most High brought the judgment. Upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal. Our forefather Jotham, a young man at the time, prophesied their destruction, and it came to pass. We read these accounts for the history, but look deeper and apply them to our lives: if there is evil being done behind closed doors, the Most High will judge it in front of everybody, like he judged Abimelech.

After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child. Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down. David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also. David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city. Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High. It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.

lawsResolved.text: If a man acts with premeditation against his neighbor, to kill him with guile, he shall die.
Killing for hire is condemned (the assassin and the one who hires him are both guilty of murder).
Government officers that engage in conspiracy, treachery and murder are to be put to death.
Warnings against an all-powerful leader, king or central government.
Punishment is the fruit and reward for iniquity and wicked ways (you shall reap that which you sow).
